newsitem.title: UK: Clearer focus sought from Pearson.
newsitem.headline: Clearer focus sought from Pearson.

text.p: Marjorie Scardino must convince investors she can impose a coherent strategy on Pearson's sprawling media and leisure empire when she takes the helm at the company next year, analysts said on Thursday.

"Pearson seems to have gone off the track. They say they want to be a media company but there are no real signs of synergy between different parts of the business," said one analyst, who declined to be named.
"What people want to see is more focus," he added.
Scardino will become chief executive of Pearson when Frank Barlow retires at the end of the year.
Scardino's appointment was greeted with scepticism by the stock market as hopes were dashed that Pearson would appoint a prominent outsider to knock the business into shape.

Scardino, 49, is currently chief executive of the Economist Group, 50 percent owned by Pearson. Profits have doubled in her three years at the Economist but she is a relative unknown for most market players. "The message that this appointment puts across is that we can expect more of the same from the company. That's not what the market wanted to hear," said the analyst.

"The market was looking for an outside appointment, someone with a big company track record. She's apparently been very successful at the Economist but it's not the same as running a major Plc," he added.

Barlow had sold off the Royal Doulton china business plus interests in wine and oil services over the past seven years to focus on the divisions of Information, Education and Entertainment over the past seven years.
But analysts say that the pieces of the jigsaw still do not fit together very well and pinpoint the Tussauds Group as a potential candidate for disposal.
The Tussauds Group includes London's famous waxwork exhibitions and theme parks in Britain and Spain.
Pearson recently agreed to sell its Westminster Press local newspaper arm to Newsquest Media Group for 305 million stg.

That sale will inflate full-year earnings but analysts are looking for pre-exceptional profits in the region of 275 million stg. The company posted a 1995 pre-tax profit of 365 million stg but this was flattered by a 131 million profit on the sale of its 9.75 direct stake in satellite broadcaster BSkyB.
Pearson retains an indirect stake of just over four percent and a newspaper report on Thursday said it may decide to sell.
"They may decide to sell if they have an acquisition they want to finance," said one analyst. The stake is worth around 440 million stg at current BSkyB prices.
Pearson also said that Dennis Stevenson, a non-executive director, was being appointed deputy chairman with immediate effect and would succeed Lord Blakenham from next May.
The changes complete a boardroom shuffle which began earlier this year when three new executive directors were appointed.
David Bell, who heads the Information division and Greg Dyke, head of Pearson television, joined the board along with John Makinson, who replaced James Joll as finance director.
